topline: Three stories today: Europe weighs what the Democrats' midterm sweep means for trade, Ukraine and its own politics; MEPs vote to soften the 2035 combustion-engine phase-out; and Czech public broadcasters strike as Babiš moves to end the licence fee.

stories.title: Europe weighs the Democrats' midterm sweep, but expects little change on tariffs
stories.summary: Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterms, passing the 218 seats needed in the House by Wednesday morning and taking Senate seats including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Maine. Trump said he would accept the results but did not see them as a verdict on him, and signalled he would use his veto. European stock indices rose modestly while defence shares such as BAE and Rheinmetall fell. Spain's Pedro Sánchez hailed the result as a sign the far right is unravelling and predicted the same in Spain's 29 November election, while European Parliament vice-president Christel Schaldemose said she was cautiously optimistic for Ukraine support and the green transition. Analysts noted that trade policy largely remains with the president, so US tariffs on Europe are unlikely to disappear.
stories.why: A Democratic Congress can push back on Ukraine aid cuts and scrutinise the White House, but the tariffs and security pressure that most affect the EU stay in Trump's hands for two more years.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage frames the result as a broad rebuke of Trump, linking it to the Iran war and fuel prices and gathering hopeful reactions from leaders who have clashed with him. Several European commentators go further and talk about the beginning of the end of Trumpism.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Global reactions roundup that ties the vote to the Iran war and petrol prices, with Sánchez and Schaldemose among the European voices.

right.angle: Right-leaning outlets focus less on the result than on Europe's response to it, presenting Sánchez and other Trump critics as making sweeping claims and accusing European media of gloating. They highlight warnings that Trump still controls foreign policy.

outlets.name: Fox News
outlets.note: Casts the European reactions, led by Sánchez's post, as bold claims from leaders already at odds with Trump.

outlets.name: Legal Insurrection
outlets.note: Collects Guardian, Spiegel and Le Monde headlines as evidence of media Schadenfreude, quoting Ischinger's call for restraint.

stories.differ: The left reads the vote as a turning point against Trumpism and a boost for Ukraine and climate policy; the right treats European enthusiasm itself as the story and stresses Trump's remaining power.

stories.title: MEPs on the environment committee vote to soften the 2035 combustion-engine phase-out
stories.summary: The European Parliament's environment committee backed a compromise on Wednesday, 48 votes to 30 with 2 abstentions, that drops the requirement for new cars to be fully zero-emission from 2035. Under the deal struck by the EPP, S&D and Renew, the fleet CO2 cut would be set at 87.5% compared with 2021, with credits such as using low-carbon EU-made steel able to raise it towards 95%; the target for vans falls to 80%. The Commission had proposed 90% last December, and France and Germany have backed 90% for the Council position. EPP rapporteur Massimiliano Salini said it would still be possible to register combustion-engine cars, while the Greens called it a bad deal. The full Parliament votes in December before talks with member states.
stories.why: It is one of the most visible rollbacks of the Green Deal and sets the Parliament's line for final negotiations on Europe's flagship car-climate law.

left.angle: Left-leaning and green-leaning coverage presents the vote as another retreat from the Green Deal brought about by car-industry pressure, stressing the Greens' objections and the risk to Europe's EV transition. We found no fresh piece from the listed left-leaning outlets on Wednesday's vote; the elDiario.es link below is earlier coverage of the Commission's original proposal.

outlets.name: elDiario.es
outlets.note: Earlier coverage: describes the Commission's U-turn as carmakers twisting Brussels's arm.

right.angle: Right-leaning outlets frame the change as common sense catching up with reality, a lifeline for carmakers and jobs, and some argue it does not go far enough because the steel credits make the rules complicated in practice.

outlets.name: El Español
outlets.note: Leads with the Parliament scrapping the petrol-and-diesel 'veto' through a cross-party pact.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (October) of the deal being struck, seen as a win for the industry.

stories.differ: The left sees a climate backslide driven by lobbying; the right sees a needed correction for industry, with some saying the compromise is still too strict.

stories.title: Czech public broadcasters strike as Babiš government moves to end the licence fee
stories.summary: Staff at Czech Television and Czech Radio went on strike on Tuesday, and thousands rallied in Prague and other cities against the government's plan to scrap the household licence fee and fund public media directly from the state budget. Under the plan the broadcasters would get about 15% less money, which unions say could mean layoffs and cancelled programmes. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said no one wants to control or nationalise public media. Press-freedom groups including the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders warned that budget funding opens the door to political pressure, and organisers expect a much larger protest at Letná on 15 November.
stories.why: Public-media independence is a core rule-of-law test under the EU's Media Freedom Act, and critics compare the plan to changes in Slovakia and Hungary that drew scrutiny from Brussels.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage frames the strike as a historic stand for press freedom, placing it in a pattern of central European governments tightening their grip on public broadcasters.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Calls the walkout historic and ties it to the government's vote to abolish the fees.

right.angle: We found no fresh right-leaning take on this week's strike. Earlier conservative coverage welcomed ending the fee as relief for households and a check on broadcasters it sees as biased towards Brussels.

outlets.name: The European Conservative
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (June): hailed scrapping the fee as a blow to 'Brussels propaganda'.

stories.differ: The left sees an attack on independent journalism; the right, in earlier coverage, saw a fee cut and a correction of broadcaster bias.
